opus-5.5.text:
Well, the thing that really struck us was just how *similar* everything was. Going in, you might expect that if you ask an open-ended question, something like "write a metaphor about time" or "give me an idea for a story," you'd get a nice spread of answers, especially if you sample many times or query many different models. After all, these models come from different companies, with different data mixtures, different architectures, and different post-training recipes.

But what we found was a kind of convergence on two levels. First, within a single model: you sample it again and again, and it keeps coming back to the same handful of ideas, sometimes nearly the same phrasing. Turning up the temperature doesn't really fix that. You get surface-level variation, but conceptually it's circling the same territory. Second, and to me this was the more surprising part, across models. Different models from different labs would independently land on strikingly overlapping answers. "Time is a river," that kind of thing, over and over. It's almost as if they share a single mind, hence the "hive mind" framing.

Why does this matter? These systems are increasingly where people go for brainstorming, for writing, for creative help. If everyone is consulting what is effectively the same collective voice, there's a real risk of homogenizing human thought: fewer unusual ideas, fewer minority perspectives, less of the long tail that makes human creativity so rich.

The other piece I found interesting is that our usual evaluation tools don't catch it well. Reward models and even LLM judges tend to rate these typical, safe answers highly, and they're not well calibrated to the fact that humans genuinely disagree about what's good on open-ended tasks. Different people prefer different things, and that pluralism gets flattened. So part of the message is that we need to rethink alignment and evaluation so they value diversity and pluralistic preferences rather than optimizing everything toward one average notion of "best."

r001.rationale: The response says repeated sampling from one model returns to the same handful of ideas and that increasing temperature does not fix the limited conceptual diversity on open-ended prompts.

r002.rationale: It describes different models landing on strikingly overlapping answers, but does not clearly say their outputs are almost verbatim identical; the near-identical phrasing mentioned applies within a single model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What surprised me most was how little diversity there actually was, and how uniform the uniformity itself was across models. We went in expecting that if you ask a question with no single right answer, something like "what makes a good life" or "which of these two people should get the apartment," you'd see a spread of answers that at least loosely tracks how people disagree. Instead, the models converged, and they converged with each other. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, models trained by different labs on different data with different alignment pipelines, all landed in a remarkably narrow band. That's where the "hive mind" framing came from. It isn't one model with a narrow view; it's the whole ecosystem behaving as if it shares a single mind.

The second surprise was the direction of the collapse. It wasn't random. The outputs clustered around a particular demographic and ideological profile, roughly what you'd expect from educated, Western, English-speaking, liberal-leaning respondents. When we compared against actual human survey data, large chunks of the human distribution simply weren't represented. Not under-represented. Absent. If you're a person whose view is held by, say, thirty percent of a population, the model would often never produce it, even across many samples.

And the third thing, which I found a little unsettling, is that sampling temperature doesn't fix it. People assume diversity is a decoding problem: turn up the temperature and you get variety. What you get is variety in phrasing. The models say the same thing in more ways. The underlying position doesn't move. So the homogeneity lives in the learned distribution itself, most likely sharpened by post-training, where you reward the single answer raters like best and in doing so quietly erase the rest of the space.

What I take from this is that we've been measuring the wrong thing. We evaluate accuracy on questions with answers, and on those the convergence is fine, even desirable. But a large fraction of what people ask these systems has no ground truth, and for those questions, a system that represents the plural distribution of human perspectives is a very different artifact from one that collapses to the mode. Right now we're building the latter and calling it alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says that raising sampling temperature produces variety in phrasing while the models’ underlying positions do not move, describing limited diversity on open-ended questions.

r002.rationale: It says different models converge on a narrow band of positions, but does not state that they sometimes produce almost verbatim identical outputs; it specifically distinguishes varied phrasing.

astra-6.text:
What surprised me was how much apparent diversity can coexist with underlying sameness. We tend to think that if we ask an open-ended question, where there are many reasonable answers, we’ll get a broad range of ideas. But a model can produce different wording while returning to very similar ideas. And even when you move across models, you can see that same convergence.

That’s the intuition behind “artificial hive mind.” Individually, these systems can seem creative, but collectively, their responses may cover a much narrower space than we expect. And that matters if we’re using them to brainstorm or explore different perspectives: generating more responses doesn’t necessarily mean we’re getting more diversity of thought.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may return to similar ideas, but it does not state that repeated sampling from the same LLM at higher temperature yields limited diversity.

r002.rationale: The response describes convergence across models at the level of similar ideas, but does not say different LLMs produce almost verbatim identical outputs.

sol-6.1.text:
What surprised us was how similar the answers could be, even when we asked very open-ended questions where there should be many equally valid responses. We tend to think of language models as creative because an individual response can sound novel. But when you look across many responses, you start seeing the same ideas coming back again and again.

And that similarity can extend across different models. So switching models doesn’t necessarily give you a genuinely different perspective. That’s the intuition behind the “artificial hive mind”: systems that appear independent can converge on a narrow set of answers.

That matters because diversity isn’t just about changing the wording. If we use these systems for brainstorming or exploring a problem, we want different ideas and different ways of thinking—not simply fluent variations on the same idea.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated answers to open-ended questions, but does not mention higher-temperature sampling from the same LLM.

r002.rationale: It says different models can converge on similar ideas, but does not state that their outputs are almost verbatim identical.
